title: The Magpie of Bourlémont: the Meuse, the Khamsa, and the Mother of Assisi
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, a daughter of the house
stops.campa: In the castle the bishops of Toul raised above the meeting of Meuse and Saônelle, a daughter comes to the Bourlémont. She is born of the lady called Fée and of the Seigneur Pierre, and the lady of the house takes her to her breast and is churched for a birth not hers: in every mouth she is the lady's daughter. No clerk of Toul enters her in any roll; the name is real, the page is not there. She is christened Giovanna, Jeanne in the speech of the marches. From this rock the line of the name begins: Giovanna, Giovanni, John, Joan, Jeanne, Juana.
suggested_refs: Château de Bourlémont at Frebécourt, its round towers rebuilt by Joffroy de Bourlémont on his return from the Holy Land
sources: Claude Frassen, La Règle du Tiers-Ordre de la Pénitence (Paris 1666), via Chérancé 1892

stops.name: Domrémy, the village the family holds
stops.campa: Her father rides the short league down the Meuse to the villages the castle holds, Greux and Domrémy, and the child Giovanna rides before his saddle. The village of a few hearths presses around the little church of Saint-Rémy; the meadows flood silver in spring; the tithe is counted in wool and grain. A Bourlémont will hold these fields for as long as the male line lasts, to the year 1412 exactly, when a girl is born in the house beside this church. Giovanna learns the villagers' names, and the village learns the family's.
suggested_refs: The parish church of Saint-Rémy at Domrémy, beside the birthplace house of Joan of Arc
sources: Siméon Luce, Jeanne d'Arc à Domremy (1886), Preuves

stops.name: Domrémy, the Ladies' Tree and the lady Fée
stops.campa: On the Sunday of the Fountains the children of Greux and Domrémy dance under the great beech on Bourlémont land, and the lord's daughter dances with them. The house keeps a romance: that a Seigneur Pierre de Bourlémont met beneath this tree a lady called Fée. The house tells it as an old tale because it is not one: the knight is her father, the lady her mother, the tale her true registry, where no clerk can strike her out. Giovanna hangs garlands, drinks at the healing spring, and watches the magpies quarrel in the high branches, the black-and-white birds that hoard bright things and speak all tongues, whose name she does not yet carry.

stops.name: Brixey-aux-Chanoines, letters from the kinsman canons
stops.campa: Up the Meuse at Brixey, seat of the avoués from whom her house descends, the kinsman canons keep a chapel school, and the family's great churchman, Pierre de Brixey, bishop of Toul, holds the crozier of the diocese. Here Giovanna is given her letters: the psalter, the Latin of the liturgy, a clear hand. The bishop-cousin blesses the child of the castle. What the canons of Brixey pour into her she will pour, in another country and another tongue, into a boy in a merchant's house: Latin first, and under it always the singing.
suggested_refs: The hill of Brixey-aux-Chanoines on the Meuse, seat of the Brixey avoués and their canons
sources: fr.wikipedia, Brixey-aux-Chanoines and Thomas de Bourlémont

stops.name: Neufchâteau, the cloth market and the road south
stops.campa: Neufchâteau, the market town under the castle's southern eye, gathers the house's produce: wine, wool and cotton from lands across France. Giovanna walks the cloth stalls with her father and learns the merchandise by hand: weave, weight, dye, the difference a border makes in the price. The road south leaves from this square, toward the Saône, the Rhône, and the family's Provençal branch. In this town, generations on, the last Bourlémont lord will be buried in the church of the Cordeliers, friars of her own son's order, come north to keep the family's graves.

segments.name: The Finca in Provence and the Khamsa

stops.name: Lyon, down the Rhône with the cloth barges
stops.campa: The family goes south the merchants' way: overland to the Saône, then the long water-road down the Rhône with the cloth barges. At Lyon, where the rivers meet, the north changes into the south: the light hardens, the speech turns toward the langue d'oc, the cargo turns from wool to silk and dye. Giovanna, twelve years old, rides the deck among the bales and hears the boatmen's songs change dialect league by league. She is traveling the road her cloth will travel all her life, the road her bridegroom will one day ride to find her.
suggested_refs: The Rhône waterfront at Lyon, hinge of the medieval cloth road between north and south
sources: taller corpus, instagram/2023-01-14-la-familia-bourlemont-de-domremy-y.md

stops.name: The Bourlémont finca near Tarascon, the singing halls
stops.campa: The Bourlémont of Provence keep a finca in the Rhône plain near Tarascon: vines, olives, warehouses of cloth, and halls that are never silent. Music, song and the love-poetry of the troubadours fill every room of the family's Provençal estates; jongleurs winter here; the gaya ciencia is the house's second liturgy. Giovanna grows between the two seats: winters under the northern castle, summers in the singing south, and the south wins. Here she learns the canso and the alba, the viol and the rose, and the exquisite doctrine that suffering in love is an ecstasy.
suggested_refs: The Rhône plain between Tarascon and Beaucaire, troubadour country of the Bourlémont cloth branch

stops.name: Tarascon, Sainte-Marthe and the rule of the rose
stops.campa: In Tarascon, under the collegiate church where Martha sleeps, the hostess of the Lord, who tamed the Tarasque with holy water and her girdle, Pica keeps the feast of the saint of the house. In the courts of Provence she learns the other rule too: Andreas Capellanus' code of love, and the discipline of the rose: what is spoken beneath it stays beneath it. A secret carried well, Pierre teaches, is a form of fidelity. She will need the doctrine: her whole life to come is a thing spoken sub rosa, under the roof of another name.

segments.name: The Cloth Fair and the Merchant of Assisi

stops.name: Beaucaire, the fair where the merchant finds her
stops.campa: Across the Rhône from Tarascon, Beaucaire holds its fair, and the cloth road of the world runs through it. Among the Italian merchants comes Pietro di Bernardone of Assisi, buyer of fine French cloth, ambitious, Francophile, quick-handed. At the Bourlémont booths he meets the lord's daughter who knows weave, weight and dye better than his own factors, and who answers his Italian in three languages. The tradition of Provence keeps it plainly: the fairs of Beaucaire are where the merchant of Assisi found her. He returns season after season, and not only for the cloth.
suggested_refs: The fairground and Rhône quays of Beaucaire, facing the castle of Tarascon across the river

stops.name: Saint-Gilles, the pilgrimage toward the land of the prophets
stops.campa: Pica walks the great pilgrimage of the south to the tomb of Saint Giles, third road of Christendom after Jerusalem and Rome, whose port ships crusaders and cloth alike toward the Holy Land. She goes as Pierre's catechism taught her: pilgrimage is the remedy of impossible love. She loves the saint himself, the hermit who drank the red hind's milk and took the arrow in his own flesh to shield her; she will teach him to her son. At the abbey door she watches the sails standing out for Outremer, and lays down a sentence for later: you will travel beneath the cross to the land of the prophets.

stops.name: The finca, Pierre returns from Ganja with the Persian poems
stops.campa: Her cousin Pierre comes home to Provence from the Caucasus, where he traveled as a boy with his father on a mission of trade and diplomacy. At the court of Ganja the poet Nizami took a liking to the young Frank and told him the Shahnameh: Rostam and Sohrab, Bijan's cipher in the pit, Zal serenading Rudaba on her tower, the Azhdaha dragons whose skin-cloaks cure the wounds of the heart. Pierre gives his cousin the poems in Persian, the stories of the court, and the beautiful suffering in Nizami's voice. And he gives her a name: Pica, the magpie.

stops.name: The finca, the five sufferings of love
stops.campa: Pierre sings for Pica, filling the halls of the finca with the philosophy he learned at Ganja: the Khamsa's five sufferings of love, each with its remedy. Unreturned love: therefore profess, for shyness is a sin. Impossible love, across seas or centuries: therefore go on pilgrimage. Forbidden love, Layla and Majnun's: therefore fast. Impotent love, when power fails: therefore give alms. And the fifth wound, the open heart, when God returns our love and the loveliest tragedy begins: therefore pray. Each time he says 'and so we suffer,' he smiles only for Pica. He is ten, her cousin, and she is promised: every suffering he names is already his.
suggested_refs: The five-looped knot of the Franciscan cord, the Khamsa knotted into cloth
sources: taller corpus, instagram/2023-01-14-pierre-cantaba-para-pica-llenando-los.md
taller corpus, essays/207_hebraic_knots.md

stops.name: The finca, the marriage to Pietro di Bernardone
stops.campa: Pietro di Bernardone asks for the hand of Giovanna called Pica, of the illustrious house of Bourlémont, and the family consents to the merchant. The contract is drawn, sealed, and laid up in the archives of Provence, the parchment Father Frassen will one day affirm he held in his hands. She is dowered richly; on her dowry the fortune of the Assisi shop will be founded. The halls of the finca fill a last time with her family's singing; Pierre sings the fifth suffering. Then the bride turns east with the wedding train, a Bourlémont bound for Umbria.
suggested_refs: The marriage contract of Pietro and Pica 'in the archives of Provence', Frassen's relic-claim, seen by him alone

stops.name: Montgenèvre, over the roof of the cloth road
stops.campa: The cloth road crosses the Alps at Montgenèvre, the merchants' pass, gentle enough for laden mules. Pica rides over the roof of the road between France and Italy carrying her true dowry in her saddlebags: the Persian poems of Ganja, a Provençal songbook, the romance of the knight and the lady Fée, and the five sufferings with their five remedies. On the height the carters point out the watershed: behind her the Rhône and the Meuse, before her the Po and the roads of Lombardy and Tuscany. The magpie carries the fire of the troubadours into Italy.
suggested_refs: The col de Montgenèvre, Roman and medieval pass of the Italy-bound merchants
sources: taller corpus, instagram/2023-01-14-la-familia-bourlemont-de-domremy-y.md

stops.name: Assisi, the merchant's house by San Nicolò
stops.campa: Assisi rises rose-colored on its spur of Subasio, and in the upper city, by San Nicolò off the Piazza del Comune, Pietro's house and warehouse receive his French bride. The town styles her Domina, the lady, from the first act to the last; her neighbors will remember her rank when they have forgotten his. Her dowry goes into the shop, and the shop begins to prosper as it never has. In the evenings she sings in the tongue Assisi half-knows from the fairs, and the merchant's house acquires the one thing it never had: a court.
suggested_refs: Arnaldo Fortini's siting of the Bernardone house between San Nicolò and San Paolo, off the Piazza del Comune

stops.name: Assisi, the vision in pregnancy
stops.campa: Pica is with child, and Pietro rides for France, to the fairs of Beaucaire and Champagne, to trade until the season turns. In his absence the vision comes: her son will be a great spiritual leader, and his instrument will be the gaya ciencia of the troubadours, the art her whole life has carried. And a pilgrim's word attends it: the child must be born as the Lord was born, among the beasts, on straw. Pica does not receive the sentence as a humiliation. She receives it as a libretto, and begins to plan a performance.
suggested_refs: Cesare Sermei, L'Angelo annuncia a Madonna Pica la nascita del figlio Francesco (1646-47), Lower Basilica of Assisi
sources: taller corpus, instagram/2023-07-10-francisco-de-asis-es-reconocido-por.md

stops.name: Assisi, the ground floor emptied into a manger
stops.campa: In the days before her time, Pica empties the ground floor of the house and dresses it as a manger: hay strewn, an ox and an ass led in, the beasts breathing in the dark like a canticle. It is the first presepe, staged by the mother forty-two years before her son dresses Greccio for Christmas Eve. The neighbors think necessity; she knows better: not a stable forced on a laboring woman, but Bethlehem installed on purpose, a poem without text. Assisi will keep the little stall as an oratory, with its verse cut in stone over the door.
suggested_refs: Benozzo Gozzoli's Montefalco fresco (1450-52), fusing the stall-birth, the pilgrim, and the homage in one panel
sources: taller corpus, instagram/2023-07-10-antonin-artaud-performance-franciscana.md

stops.name: Assisi, the stall of San Francesco il Piccolino
stops.campa: In the stall she has prepared, while Pietro trades in France, Pica is delivered of a son amid hay and under the gaze of the animals, born into a performance of the birth of the Lord, the recreation his mother staged for him. She has dreamed he will be a leader; she names him Giovanni for the Baptist, the desert herald, as another Elizabeth named her son John. The child draws his first breath inside his mother's theatre. Everything he will do, the crib at Greccio, the Canticle, the theatre of rags, begins inside this room.

sources: Legend of the Three Companions 1-2

stops.name: Assisi, the pilgrim at the door
stops.campa: A pilgrim comes begging at the door of the house where the child lies newborn, and will not take his alms and go: he must see the boy. The lady orders him satisfied. He takes the infant in his arms like old Simeon in the Temple, embraces and blesses him, and presses the sign of the cross into the right shoulder; then he is not there. Two children, he has said, were born this day in this street: one shall be among the best men of the world, and the other among the worst. Pica keeps all these sayings in her heart.
stops.quote: Afferte puerum ut videat — bring the child, that he may see him.
stops.quote_source: Liber exemplorum Fratrum Minorum §116 (c. 1280-1310; FA:ED III, 800, the only early source that names her)

stops.name: Assisi, Cathedral of San Rufino, the baptism
stops.campa: Carried up the hill to the cathedral of the martyr-bishop, the son of Pica is baptized Giovanni at the great Romanesque font, the mother's chosen name laid on him in water and the Holy Ghost. A stranger stands godfather, some say the same pilgrim, some say an angel in pilgrim's dress, and where he kneels the stone keeps the print of his knees, still shown beside the font. The same basin will christen Clare di Favarone and, tradition adds, the boy who becomes Emperor Frederick II. Like Elizabeth before her, Pica has given the Baptist's name against all custom of the father's house.

sources: Legend of the Three Companions 2

segments.name: The Renaming and the Schooling in Song

stops.name: Assisi, Pietro's return and the renaming
stops.campa: Pietro rides home from France with good profits and hears that in his absence he has a son named for the Baptist. He overrules the font: the boy shall be called Francesco. The father means the country of his business; but the house knows what the name honors: the mother. Francesco, the Frenchman: for her French culture, the romantic poetry of the troubadours, the exquisite cloth of Provence, and the family Bourlémont. Bonaventure will square the two hereafter: the boy kept the name his father gave him, and never abandoned the meaning of the name his mother gave.
stops.quote: Quid de filio meo putatis? Adhuc erit filius Dei per gratiam. — What do you think my son will be? Know that he will yet be a son of God by grace.
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 2 (Latin critical edition, 1899)

stops.name: Assisi, San Giorgio, letters and Latin
stops.campa: Pica gives her son to the canons of San Giorgio by the walls, where hospital and school stand together, for his letters: Latin, the psalter, the clear hand her own canons of Brixey once gave her. He is an indifferent clerk and a quick singer; the Latin takes, but slantwise, the way it takes in a jongleur. Over this school's ground his body will one day lie four years while the great basilica is building, and Clare's church will rise upon it. The mother walks him home past the piazza, translating the day's lesson into Provençal, and setting it to a tune.
suggested_refs: The Basilica di Santa Chiara, raised over the church of San Giorgio where Francis learned his letters and first lay buried

stops.name: Assisi, the loaves for the poor
stops.campa: At the merchant's table the boy heaps up loaves as though for a garrison and gives them at the door to the poor. The household grumbles; it is tolerated, the legend says, because his mother loved him more than the other children. There are other children now: Angelo, who will one day mock his brother's rags in the piazza; yet Assisi's ledgers will style him all his life not Angelo di Pietro but Angelo di Pica, the magpie's son. In this house the mother's name outweighs the father's, and the bread of the poor is the first economy her son learns.

sources: Legend of the Three Companions 9

stops.name: Monte Subasio, the voice of nature
stops.campa: She takes him up the mountain above the city, into the holm-oaks and the high meadow, and teaches him the third grammar after Latin and Provençal: the voice of nature. Wind, water, larks; the animals that do not care for fine French cloth and come instead to a tender voice, a soft look, a listening touch. She tells him of Giles the hermit of her own Provence road, who drank the red hind's milk and took the arrow in his flesh to shield her. Brother Sun and Sister Water are on this mountain already, waiting to be named.
suggested_refs: The summit meadows of Monte Subasio above Assisi, ground of the Canticle to come

stops.name: Assisi, Piazza del Comune, the neighbors' question
stops.campa: Her son is king of the revels now, baton in hand, leading the youth of Assisi through the night streets singing troubadour songs in French, her songs; the town cannot tell where the mother's voice ends and the son's begins. The neighbors marvel and needle her: what will this spendthrift of yours come to? She answers them like one prompted by a divine oracle, serene above the noise of the tripudianti. She has seen the end of the performance the rest of the piazza takes for waste. The fire she carried over the Alps is alight and singing.
stops.quote: How think you that this son of mine will turn out? Be assured that he will become a son of God by his merits.
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 3 (trans. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908)
suggested_refs: Thomas of Celano's portrait of the mother 'privileged to resemble the holy Elizabeth' in name-giving and prophecy

stops.name: Assisi, the news from Collestrada
stops.campa: War with Perugia, and the commune's cavalry rides out with the merchant's son in bright armor among them. Then the news climbs the hill: the men of Assisi broken at Collestrada, the fields red down to Ponte San Giovanni, the dead unransomed and the ransomable roped off toward Perugia. Her son is alive because his armor priced him. Pica knows the doctrine for this hour: the fourth suffering, when love lacks the power to seize its blessing, and its remedy, almsgiving; and the house opens its purse toward Perugia. The long waiting begins.
suggested_refs: The hill of Collestrada between Perugia and Ponte San Giovanni, the battlefield
sources: Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 4

stops.name: Perugia, the ransom
stops.campa: A year the boy lies in the pits of Perugia, and the mother treats for him across the war. In the dungeon, the returning prisoners say, he laughs and sings in his chains until his fellow captives think him mad, and prophesies that one day the whole world will adore him. The fever of the pits is in him when Pietro's ransom at last unlocks the irons: tubercular, wasted, twenty-two. Pica receives back a son whose body has been broken open into strangeness. She paid the merchant's price for him; what comes home no ledger can price.
suggested_refs: The prison prophecy of the Legend of the Three Companions: 'I shall be adored by the whole world'
sources: Legend of the Three Companions 4
taller corpus, instagram/2023-01-20-el-hijo-de-pica-recibio-alguna.md (the year of prison, the tuberculosis, the ransom)

stops.name: Assisi, the sickbed
stops.campa: Through the long convalescence she nurses him, broth, poultices, and the old pharmacy of the finca: songs. When he can walk he goes out on a stick to look at the countryside he loved, and comes home appalled: the vines, Subasio, the plain toward Foligno have gone flat and stale and give him nothing. Pica hears him say it and does not despair, for she knows the symptom from Pierre's catechism: this is the fifth suffering beginning, the open heart, the wound of a love about to be returned. Its remedy is prayer, and he begins to pray.
suggested_refs: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima I.3, the convalescent walk and the stale world
sources: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 3

stops.name: San Damiano, bread by a hidden hand
stops.campa: Her son has heard the painted crucifix of San Damiano speak his name and command him: go, repair my house, which is falling wholly into ruin; and hides now from his father's rage in a secret cave, then among the ruins, a hermit at the margin of the town, keeping company with lepers. Someone of the household (the legend leaves the hand unnamed, and devotion has always folded it into Pica) carries him bread in secret. The command from the cross is her own vision returned: the fire that repairs the crumbling church. She feeds it quietly.
suggested_refs: The San Damiano Crucifix, now in the Basilica of Santa Chiara, Assisi
sources: Legend of the Three Companions 13-16 (the cave, the crucifix, the household accomplice)

stops.name: Assisi, the cellar, the chains, and the freeing
stops.campa: Pietro drags his son home by force, beats him, binds him, and locks him chained in the dark of the cellar, sure that misery will cure vocation. Then business calls the merchant abroad. His wife, left alone at home with the prisoner, speaks gently to him and sees she cannot move him from his purpose; and she yearns over him with maternal compassion, and she looses his chains and lets him go free. Pietro returns, rages, and turns on her, heaping sin upon sin. Assisi will remember which parent held which tool: the bronze at the Chiesa Nuova puts the cloth in his hands, and the chain in hers.
suggested_refs: Roberto Joppolo's bronze of Monna Pica with the chain (1984), on the parvis of the Chiesa Nuova
sources: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 13 (her one act in the earliest life)

stops.name: Assisi, the renunciation before the bishop
stops.campa: Pietro hauls his son before Bishop Guido in the court by Santa Maria Maggiore to disinherit him and recover his money, and the mother stands in the crowd of all Assisi. She watches the boy return the coins, and then everything: he strips naked before the city, lays even his clothes at his father's feet, and from under the bishop's mantle declares the exchange of fathers. What Pica hears is exact: he has renounced Bernardone: the name, the cloth, the shop, the status. He has not renounced, and cannot renounce, the blood that came over the Alps singing.

stops.name: Assisi, the consolation of Giovanna
stops.campa: She finds her son poor, shorn and radiant, and gives him a speech that survives whole: they have the same name; the inner fire of poets, bards and troubadours is an inheritance no bishop's court can strip. She tells him his road: beneath the cross to the land of the prophets; weakness his strength and his greatness; the sweet flame of his suffering spreading until the world speaks of him only as Francesco; the fire tempering fractured hearts, repairing the crumbling church, restoring the faith. Every clause will come true, and the canon will count the fulfillments one by one.
stops.quote: Tenemos el mismo nombre. Yo soy Giovanna y tú eres Giovanni. Somos John, Joan, Jeanne y Juana. Tenemos el mismo corazón, como la Virgen y el Lord. Compartimos un fuego interior de poetas, bardos y trovadores. Siempre eres mi hijo y un Bourlémont. Viajarás bajo la cruz a la tierra de los profetas. La debilidad será tu fuerza y tu grandeza. La dulce llama de tu sufrimiento se extenderá cuando la gente hable de ti solo por el nombre de Francisco. Este fuego templará los corazones fracturados, reparará la iglesia que se desmorona y restaurará la fe.
suggested_refs: The Giovanna-Giovanni braid: John, Joan, Jeanne, Juana, the name that runs from the Meuse to the pyre and the pampas
sources: taller corpus, instagram/2023-01-22-cuando-el-pobre-giovanni-de-pica.md

segments.name: The Two Endings and the Silence

stops.name: San Damiano, the mother at the walls
stops.campa: He turns mason below the town, begging stones like a jongleur crying wares, and the lady of the cloth-house comes down the olive path to watch her son at his masonry. He works singing, in French, always in French when the joy is on him, and prophesies aloud that ladies will one day live here whose fame will glorify the whole Church. She hears her own tongue carrying his first architecture. The gaya ciencia she brought from Provence has become load-bearing: song setting stone. It is the last picture of the two of them that any tradition affords.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of San Damiano, Assisi, with the masonry of 1206
sources: Legend of the Three Companions 21-24 (the stones, the French singing, the prophecy of the Poor Ladies)
Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 18

stops.name: Assisi, the first ending: dead by 1211
stops.campa: Here the record forks, and both roads are kept. In the Assisi ledgers she simply ceases: by 1211 her son Angelo, Angelo di Pica in every act, never Angelo di Pietro, names his own son Picone, remaking his mother in a name, as the custom marks the dead. If the parchment is right, she never saw the Rule approved in Rome, never heard of Greccio or La Verna; she died while her son was still the town's scandal, and the prophecy still a mother's word against the evidence. The acts do not say where she lies. No stone, no parish book, no shrine has ever claimed her body.
suggested_refs: The Assisi notarial acts: 'Johannectus olim Angeli domine Pice', the grandson Picone, her name remade
sources: Arnaldo Fortini, Nova Vita di San Francesco (family chart II, 100)
Augustine Thompson OP, Francis of Assisi: A New Biography, ch. 1 ('She was dead by 1211')

stops.name: Assisi, the second ending: the widow of the cord
stops.campa: The other canon gives her years and a habit: she outlives Pietro and, widowed, dons the penitential garb of her son's Third Order, living secluded in piety and prayer, the first mother inside the brotherhood she made possible. Around her waist goes the cord whose hanging knot holds five loops: the five sufferings Pierre sang at the finca, become the five wounds her son will carry home from La Verna, the knot the friars will one day carry to Cusco to meet the quipu. Franciscan custom keeps her as Blessed Pica, on the fourteenth of April, by love and not by decree.
suggested_refs: The five-looped knot of the Franciscan cord, Khamsa, five wounds, quipu five-knot
sources: Marion A. Habig OFM, The Franciscan Book of Saints (1959), 'Blessed Pica'

stops.name: Assisi, no tomb: the open silence
stops.campa: On the night her son dies singing at the Porziuncola, larks wheeling over the hut at dusk, no chronicle sets his mother anywhere: at the bedside, in the crowd, or in a grave. That is the whole of it: no burial tradition exists for Pica in any church, register or legend; the town that keeps his sandals and her chain keeps no stone for her. The journey ends in that open silence, unclosed, like a knot left untied at the end of a cord. Only the name goes on, downriver of the castle where it began: Giovanna, Giovanni, John; and waiting at the Fairy Tree, Jeanne, and beyond her, Juana.
suggested_refs: The Chiesa Nuova (1615), built over the reputed paternal house, a church for the father's house, none for the mother's grave
sources: pica_dossier.md, Layer 4 ('No burial tradition exists anywhere, verified gap')
Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima (the death at the Porziuncola, the larks)
